'''Franciszek Leja''' ({{small|Polish:}} {{IPAc-pl|f|r|a|n|'|ć|i|sz|e|k|-|'|l|e|j|a}}; 27 January 1885 in [[Grodzisko Górne]] near [[Leżajsk]] &ndash; 11 October 1979 in [[Kraków]], Poland) was a Polish [[mathematician]] known for his work in [[analytic functions]] and [[topology]]. He was one of the leading representatives of the [[Kraków School of Mathematics]].<ref name="Wójcik">{{cite web|url=https://gigancinauki.pl/gn/biogramy/84811,Leja-Franciszek.html |language=pl |author=Wiesław Wójcik |title=Leja Franciszek |website=gigancinauki.pl |access-date=5 August 2026}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Leja was born in 1885 as the son of Jan Leja and Elżbieta ({{nee|Majkut}}). He grew up on a farm in the small village of [[Grodzisko Górne]], in southeastern Poland.<ref name="MatHist">{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Leja/ |title=Franciszek Leja |work=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive |author=J.J. O'Connor and E.F. Robertson |access-date=5 August 2026}}</ref> Between 1896‒1904, he attended a [[gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]] in [[Jarosław]]. After completing his secondary education, Leja matriculated at the Department of Philosophy of the [[Jan Kazimierz University]] (now the [[University of Lviv]] in [[Ukraine]]). In 1909, he started working as a teacher of mathematics and physics in secondary schools from 1910 to 1923, including in [[Kraków]].<ref name="Kosek">{{cite web|url=https://repozytorium.biblos.pk.edu.pl/redo/resources/29798/file/suwFiles/KosekM_FewFacts.pdf |title=A Few Facts Concerning the Outstanding Polish Mathematician Franciszek Leja |author=Marta Kosek |work=Technical Transactions |date=2015 |access-date=6 August 2026}}</ref> In 1913, Leja travelled to London, where he attended [[Alfred North Whitehead]]’s lectures.<ref name="MatHist"></ref> 

Following the outbreak of [[World War I]], Leja enlisted in the [[Polish Legions in World War I|Polish Legions]] but resigned when it was required of him to swear an oath of allegiance to Austria.<ref name="Kosek"></ref> In 1916, he earned his [[doctorate]] at the [[Jagiellonian University]] based on the thesis entitled ''Własności niezmiennicze równań różniczkowych ze względu na przekształcenia stycznościowe'' (Invariant Properties of Differential Equations with Respect to Contact Transformations) written under the supervision of [[Kazimierz Żorawski]].<ref name="Wójcik"></ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=60303 |title=Franciszek Leja |work=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=6 August 2026}}</ref> From 1924 to 1936, he was a professor at the [[Warsaw University of Technology]] and the [[University of Warsaw]], and from 1936 to 1960 at the [[Jagiellonian University]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kleiner|first=W.|year=1985|title=Franciszek Leja|url=http://pldml.icm.edu.pl/pldml/element/bwmeta1.element.desklight-7acb1961-3505-4591-892b-b1e59f5590dd|journal=[[Annales Polonici Mathematici]]|volume=46|issue=1|pages=1–11|doi=10.4064/ap-46-1-1-11 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=60303}}</ref>

In 1919, Leja co-founded the Mathematical Society (transformed the following year into the [[Polish Mathematical Society]]). He served as its secretary from 1919 until 1921.<ref name="Kosek"></ref> In 1931, he became a member of the [[Warsaw Scientific Society|Warsaw Science Society]] (TNW). In 1939, he travelled to France where he delivered lectures for the [[French Mathematical Society]].<ref name="MatHist"></ref>

During [[World War II]], Leja was captured by German Nazis in the ''[[Sonderaktion Krakau]]'' operation and sent with 183 Polish professors of the [[Jagiellonian University]] and [[AGH University of Science and Technology|University of Technology]] to [[Sachsenhausen concentration camp]]. After international protest by prominent Italians including [[Benito Mussolini]] and the [[Apostolic Palace|Vatican]], 101 professors who were older than 40 were released from Sachsenhausen on February 8, 1940. Leja was not in the group of released prisoners as he was older than 40. He stayed in the concentration camp until May 1940 when he returned to Kraków. In Kraków, Leja found that the university had been closed and his apartment had been taken over by the Nazis. Homeless and with no income, he decided to move to Grodzisko Górne where he and his wife, Janina,<ref name="Kosek"></ref>  had a small house and garden. They got a permission from Gestapo and left Kraków. In Grodzisko, Leja wrote the book on the calculus ''Rachunek różniczkowy i całkowy ze wstępem do równań różniczkowych''.

In 1948, Leja began working for the [[Institute of Mathematics of the Polish Academy of Sciences|Institute of Mathematics]], which was incorporated into the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] in 1952.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.impan.pl/en/insitute/about-us/history |title=History |website=impan.pl |access-date=7 December 2024 |archive-date=25 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241225182045/https://www.impan.pl/en/insitute/about-us/history |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1958, Leja was an invited speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] organized in Edinburgh delivering a lecture titled ''Sur les moyennes arithmétiques, géométriques et harmoniques des distances mutuelles des points d’un ensemble''.<ref name="Kosek"></ref> In the period of 1963–1965, Leja served as president of the [[Polish Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bcpw.bg.pw.edu.pl/Content/850/sylw_prof_035.pdf |language=pl |title=FRANCISZEK LEJA (1885—1979) |website=bcpw.bg.pw.edu.pl |author=Teresa Kempa-Englert |access-date=6 August 2026}}</ref>

His main scientific interests concentrated on [[analytic functions]], in particular the method of extremal points and transfinite diameters. He was also interested in [[differential equation|differential equations]], [[interpolation space|interpolation theory]]<ref name="Kosek"></ref> and [[topology]]; he introduced the definition of [[topological group]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Handbook of the History of General Topology, Tom 3|last=C.E. Aull and R. Lowen|publisher=Kluwer Academic Publisher|year=2001|isbn=0-7923-6970-X|location=Dordrecht|pages=1031}}</ref> In pluripotential theory, together with his student, {{ill|Józef Karol Siciak|pl|Józef Karol Siciak}}, he introduced the Leja-Siciak extremal function.<ref name="Kosek"></ref>

==Works==
* ''Rachunek różniczkowy i całkowy ze wstępem do równań różniczkowych'', first edition in 1947, Polish Mathematical Society, 17 edition in 2008 PWN.
* ''Funkcje zespolone'' (pub. 1967, pub. 5 1979).
* ''Teoria funkcji analitycznych'', PWN, Warszawa 1957.

==Honours==
*Commander's Cross of the [[Order of Polonia Restituta]] (1959)<ref>{{cite book | last = Duda | first = Roman | title = Matematycy XIX i XX wieku związani z Polską | trans-title= 19th and 20th-Century Mathematicians Connected to Poland | publisher = Wydawnictwo Uniwersytetu Wrocławskiego | location = Wrocław | year = 2012 | pages = 257–261 | language = pl}}</ref>
*[[Medal of the 10th Anniversary of People's Poland]] (1955)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dziennikustaw.gov.pl/mp/1955/s/101/1400 |language=pl |title=Monitor Polski 1955 r. nr 101, poz. 1400 |website=dziennikustaw.gov.pl |access-date=6 August 2026}}</ref>
*Officer's Cross of the [[Order of Polonia Restituta]] (1954)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dziennikustaw.gov.pl/mp/1954/s/112/1588 |title=Monitor Polski 1954 r. nr 112, poz. 1588 |website=dziennikustaw.gov.pl |access-date=6 August 2026}}</ref>
